summary.title: Visualizing Algorithms
summary.one_liner: Learn how visualizing algorithms (best-candidate and Bridson Poisson-disc sampling, Fisher–Yates shuffle, random-comparator shuffle bias, quicksort and mergesort) reveals their behavior and bias.
keywords: how to shuffle an array randomly
why random sort comparator is broken
takeaways: Best-candidate sampling picks the farthest of several random candidates, giving better spread than uniform random sampling; Bridson's algorithm gives Poisson-disc spacing in linear time.
Fisher–Yates is an unbiased, linear-time, constant-space shuffle, while sorting with a random comparator produces biased, non-random orderings.
A single run can look random while hiding bias, so visualizations must be designed around the specific question (e.g., an index probability matrix).
Static displays (key frames, dense breadth-first quicksort rows, colored threads) can be scanned faster than animations.
Visualization helps with teaching, debugging, and learning algorithms, complementing tests rather than replacing them.
summary.summary: Mike Bostock's essay uses interactive visualizations to explain several algorithms: sampling methods (uniform random, Mitchell's best-candidate, and Bridson's Poisson-disc sampling) judged by Voronoi-cell area, shuffling (Fisher–Yates versus a flawed random-comparator sort, assessed with an empirical bias matrix), and sorting (quicksort and mergesort) shown as animations and static key-frame displays. Code snippets in JavaScript accompany each algorithm, with explanations of trade-offs like candidate count and brute-force versus quadtree nearest-neighbor search. The closing section argues for visualization's value in entertainment, teaching, debugging, and learning, and begins a classification of visualizations by the derived data they show, starting with black-box output. The page text is cut off before that classification is finished.
